title: Body, soul, mind
hook: the body senses, the soul desires, the mind rules (Meditations 3.16)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Meditations, the notebook Marcus doubted he'd reread. Your line was help yourself now.

Plato pictured the soul as a chariot: a driver and two winged horses, one pulling well and one pulling wild. Marcus Aurelius, closing his third book, offers a plainer picture, with no horses at all. A person, he says, is three things: a body, a soul, and a mind, each with its own job. Then a harder question: which of those jobs belongs to the good person alone? His answer takes a surprising route. Today: body, soul, mind.
screen: `A CHARIOT, A DRIVER, TWO HORSES.` → `MARCUS: THREE THINGS.` → `WHICH JOB IS YOURS ALONE?`

segments.voice: To the body, Marcus writes, belong the senses. To the soul, which for him means the life force that wants and moves, belong the impulses. To the mind belong the principles. Then he checks each job against who else has it. Receiving impressions through the senses? Cattle do that. Being yanked around by desire? Wild animals do that, he says, and so did tyrants like Phalaris and Nero. Even using the mind to pursue what seems useful? People who betray their country and do anything behind closed doors do that too. None of the three, by itself, makes a good person. So what belongs to the good person alone? To welcome what happens and what's woven for them; to keep the spirit within untroubled, undisturbed by a crowd of impressions; to follow it quietly, as a god; never to say anything false or do anything unjust. This isn't contempt for the body. Marcus is sorting jobs, not condemning them. His point is about who drives. Senses report. Desires pull. Principles decide. When the order flips, and the pull decides, things go badly. That closes book three. It began with time running short, and it ends with the one thing worth spending that time on: a mind that keeps its own counsel, honestly, whatever comes.
screen: `SENSES, IMPULSES, PRINCIPLES.` · `CATTLE, BEASTS AND TRAITORS SHARE THEM.` · `WHAT'S LEFT: WELCOME, CALM, TRUTH.` · `WHO DRIVES?` · then, large: `THREE PARTS.`

segments.voice: Check in with each of the three: first the body, what are your senses reporting, warmth, an ache, the sound in the room? Then the part that wants: what's pulling at you right now, food, your phone, a worry, a person? Then the mind: choose one principle to steer by for the next hour, and let it take the reins, gently.
Body, soul, mind. Marcus says the body senses, the soul desires, the mind holds principles, and the good person lets the mind steer. Today's word.
Your line: three parts. Senses report, desires pull, principles decide who drives. Book three, done.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes use Meditations 3.16 as a quick check-in: what the body senses, what the soul wants, and which principle the mind will steer by.

myth: Marcus says the body and desire are evil
he's sorting what each part does; his point is about which part steers.
Marcus says even traitors use the mind to pursue what seems useful
so the mind's cleverness alone doesn't make a good person.
book three ends here, before the fire of book four.

fork.setup: you're tired, a craving is pulling hard, and your mind already knows what it wants to do. who gets the reins, in 3.16?
options: the impulse: it's strongest right now.
the mind, steering by a principle.
fork.reveal: Marcus: senses report, impulses pull, principles decide. the good person's part is letting the mind drive.

original.note: Greek: body, soul, mind, the three parts Marcus names in 3.16.

trapdoor: what you thought: the mind should control the body.
what it means: senses and desires belong even to animals and tyrants; what's yours alone is welcoming what comes and keeping truth and justice.
what a scholar hears: Marcus's soma, psyche, nous gives the 'soul' the impulses and keeps 'mind' for the ruling part, a three-part scheme he uses again in 12.3.
recall: taught: carry home something good daily
guess: the part of you that senses, in Marcus's three parts
the part of you that wants, and must be made to obey
the only part of you that truly matters to Marcus

chat.says: In Marcus's three parts, what belongs to the good person alone?
options: Welcoming what comes, keeping the spirit within calm, never saying false or doing unjust.
Sharp senses and a strong body, since cattle and beasts lack proper reason.
Using the mind cleverly to get what seems useful, which animals can never do.
chat.meaning: Cattle sense, beasts and tyrants are pulled by desire, even traitors use the mind; the good person's own part is welcome, calm and truth.

Plato.meaning: Athenian philosopher who pictured the soul as a chariot

Phalaris.meaning: an ancient tyrant Marcus names beside Nero

Nero.meaning: a Roman emperor Marcus names as ruled by desire

Marcus Aurelius.meaning: Roman emperor and Stoic who wrote notes to himself

notes: 3.16 paraphrased: body, soul, intelligence; to the body belong sensations, to the soul appetites (impulses), to the intelligence principles; receiving impressions belongs also to cattle; being pulled by desire to wild beasts, to effeminate men, to Phalaris and Nero; having the intelligence guide to what seems suitable to those who don't believe in gods, betray their country, and do their impure deeds behind closed doors; what is peculiar to the good man is to be pleased and content with what happens, not defile the divinity within, keep it tranquil, following it as a god, saying nothing contrary to truth, doing nothing contrary to justice. Confirm.
Plato's chariot image is a chariot with a charioteer and two winged horses (Phaedrus); the hook says 'carriage' loosely. Confirm acceptable.
3.16 as the last entry of book three: confirm against Long's numbering.
The trapdoor's claim about Marcus's tripartite soma/psyche/nous as a later Stoic usage: confirm wording.
